author: TGEU
title: Trans activists and stakeholders gather at TGEU’s Pre-Council to advance trans rights in Eastern Europe and Central Asia
content:
On 9-10 September in Ljubljana, Slovenia, 27 trans activists from Eastern Europe and Central Asia (EECA) and international stakeholders came together to ask one question: how do we protect trans people in a region where democracy and human rights are deteriorating?




The second TGEU Pre-Council Strategic Meeting on Trans Rights in EECA took place ahead of TGEU’s 10th European and Central Asian Trans Council. Over two days, participants analysed the rapidly changing political and legal environment, exchanged lessons learned, and explored ways to strengthen cooperation, joint advocacy and coordinated action.

 




The Strategic Meeting brought together three groups with different but complementary types of expertise and mandates: 







EECA trans activists with direct experience working with communities and conducting national advocacy




International stakeholders working on human rights and the rule of law




Allied movement leaders engaged in human rights protection.







Together, they aimed to build a shared understanding of key challenges and possible responses, identify political and legal leverage points for 2026–2027, and strengthen trust and cooperation.



















Key takeaways







Participants shared strategies for responding to anti-trans policies.

author: TGEU
title: Join the HIV Awareness Week in Berlin to establish the Emergency Support Network
content:
We are organising two free-of-charge parallel training programmes for queer and trans people that will come together on Friday, 20 November, to establish the Emergency Support Network.




This network should help people navigate services, identify realistic pathways to HIV prevention and care, and receive support without having to navigate complex systems alone. We also want to recognise that Ballroom houses, queer and trans collectives, and migrant communities already provide essential care infrastructure. We intend to strengthen these existing relationships, rather than create a parallel system disconnected from the communities themselves.




The initiative is particularly focused on two target audience groups:







Queer and trans people living with HIV who face barriers to accessing healthcare, especially those without health insurance, appropriate documentation, or access to HIV treatment and other essential services.




Queer and trans people on the move, including migrants, refugees, asylum seekers and undocumented people, who face difficulties accessing healthcare, HIV prevention, testing, PrEP, PEP and treatment.







Community HIV Training — 16, 18 and 20 November




This programme is intended for queer and trans adults, particularly queer and trans youth aged 18 and over, migrants, refugees, asylum seekers, undocumented people and other people on the move.




It is especially relevant to queer and trans people who are living with HIV and face difficulties accessing treatment or healthcare, as well as those who need access to HIV prevention, testing, PrEP, PEP and other sexual health services.




The sessions will be interactive and community-led, covering HIV prevention and care, PrEP, PEP, testing, treatment, U=U, sexual health, pleasure, harm reduction and navigating healthcare systems.




An important feature is that registration for this programme is anonymous.

 Participants are not asked to provide their names, email addresses or HIV status. Anyone who wants to receive practical information or reminders can voluntarily register their email address through a separate form, which is not linked to their anonymous demographic responses.




This distinction is particularly important for people who may be reluctant to engage with services or activities because of concerns about confidentiality, stigma or their migration status.










register here










Health Champions Training — 17, 19 and 20 November




This programme is designed for trans and queer community leaders, particularly people involved in Ballroom houses, collectives and grassroots networks.




The training follows a train-the-trainer approach and will cover HIV, STIs and other infectious diseases prevention, treatment and sexual and reproductive health knowledge, and other topics like U=U, harm reduction, structural barriers to healthcare, peer education and safe healthcare navigation.




Participants will work through practical exercises such as community mapping, HIV knowledge games, real-life scenarios, role-play and referral mapping. The objective is to equip them to become trusted points of connection between their communities and healthcare services, while recognising that Health Champions are not expected to act as clinicians, legal experts or crisis responders.




On the final day, Health Champions will meet healthcare professionals, service providers and participants from the other training programme to help establish practical referral pathways and community-based support structures.










register here










Building the Emergency Support Network 

—

 

20 November 




On Friday, participants from both programmes will come together with healthcare professionals, community organisations and service providers.




The aim is to establish direct connections between people who need support, trusted community leaders and organisations capable of providing services. Participants will learn what support is available, who can access it, what barriers remain and how to make safe referrals.




The week will culminate in 

Under the Jellicle Moon Kiki Ball on Saturday, 21 November

, celebrating Ballroom culture, community leadership and the relationships developed throughout the initiative.




Note: 

All workshop participants must be 18 or older and attend all three days of their respective training. Snacks and dinner will be provided each day.




Your support makes change possible




We work across Europe and Central Asia to advance trans rights, build strong communities, and drive change through research, advocacy, and community-building.




Your donation helps us continue this vital work — defending trans lives, amplifying trans voices, and advocating for justice every day.

author: TGEU
title: The Trans Leaders Academy 2026-27 kicks off
content:
We are delighted to introduce the inspiring 

Trans Leaders Academy

 Cohort 2026–27. Over the coming year, the 16 leaders will take part in virtual and in-person trainings and peer exchange sessions.




To further strengthen their practice, they will also have the opportunity to join the Spring 

Leadership Kitchen Series

,

 a six-month coaching space made possible through a partnership between TGEU and 

Spring

. Through the coaching, they will have space to reflect, share and grow in leadership while connecting with a wider community of global change-makers from diverse social and ecological justice movements.




We are excited to welcome this group and to witness their leadership journeys as they reflect, share and grow in community.




Meet the Trans Leaders Academy 2026–2027 cohort:













Alia Lehner (she/her)

 was born and raised in Austria. She is the State Secretary and Queer Representative of the Young Generation (JG) Upper Austria, and the State Secretary and Transgender Spokesperson of the SoHo Upper Austria.

Change-making  leadership vision:

To build an inclusive, courageous, and intersectional movement where trans people are empowered to lead, shape political decisions, and create lasting social change.



















Beatriz Carmo Flores (she/her)

 is an activist and community organiser based in Portugal. As a Coordinator at GRIT, the trans reflection and intervention group of ILGA Portugal, she supports and strengthens community organising, from peer-support spaces to public advocacy.

Change-making vision:

To build collective power through community care, so that trans communities can lead the change for human rights while impacting positively each other’s lives and thrive together.



















Evi Gümüssoy (they/them)

 is from Turkey and works on the TIN* & Refugees team at the TransInterQueer (TrIQ) organisation in Berlin. 

Change-making leadership vision:

To transform these shared lived experiences into collective power by building community-rooted support networks that protect our sustainability, mental well-being, and joy.



















Jononi Zulaikho (she/her)

 is a poet and artist actively contributing to Colored Qollective through translation and creating and holding space for trans and queer communities.

Change-making leadership vision:

To hear and see one another, speak openly about our differences and the privileges that shape our experiences, while remembering that, despite our differences, we remain connected in different ways and are part of a larger whole.



















Mak Maslać (he/him)

 is a writer, editor and cultural worker based in Zagreb, Croatia. He is the editor-in-chief of VoxFeminae, a queer feminist online magazine focused on culture and societal phenomena, where he also writes on queer and feminist topics, literature and popular culture.

Change-making leadership vision:

To create and protect spaces for more open, critical and nuanced conversations about culture, queerness, sexuality and BDSM through writing, publishing and community work.



















Maui Angela Miranda

 

(she/her)

 is a writer, editor and cultural worker based in Zagreb, Croatia. He is the editor-in-chief of VoxFeminae, a queer feminist online magazine focused on culture and societal phenomena, where he also writes on queer and feminist topics, literature and popular culture.

Change-making leadership vision:

To create sustainable systems of care that center racialized trans migrants. I aim to cultivate “care-full” spaces where trans individuals can heal from systemic racism while building collective resilience and joy.



















Miia Kovanen (she/her)

 is from Tampere, Finland. In this project, she represents Transfeminiinit Ry / Transfeminines NGO. She works in the organisation under the title of a volunteer social assistant. She is also a member of the feminist organisation Naisasialiitto Unioni / The Finnish Women’s Association Unioni.

Change-making leadership vision:

To take on this new role given to her. Indeed, she has only been in the sphere of advocacy for a relatively short while. Her journey has necessitated rapid personal development, which she aims to continue in these new responsibilities.













Nederland, Amsterdam, 20240925
Natsumi Kaori
foto: Kick Smeets (c) ‘24







Natsumi Hernandez

 

(she/her)

 is a transgender activist, model, runway coach, and personal stylist originally from Nicaragua. Since 2014, she has worked in human rights and transgender advocacy, collaborating with organisations such as USAID and local initiatives supporting vulnerable members of the LGBTIQ+ community.

Change-making leadership:

Creating safe spaces for her community, for her trans siblinx who are undocumented, experiencing addiction, or facing mental health challenges.



















Pie Formosa (they/them)

 is a Chinese human rights defender, non-binary activist and refugee based in Brussels, Belgium. They coordinate Protect Human Rights Defenders (PHRD.EU) and are part of TGEU’s Trans Refugee Network, working across trans liberation, refugee justice, democracy, accessibility and resistance to transnational repression.

Change-making leadership vision:

To turn survival into solidarity and lived experience into collective power  ensuring that those most affected can shape the systems, policies and movements that govern their lives.






















Queen Kevhoney Scarlett (she/her)

 is a visionary leader based in France, representing Miss Trans Global and Inspiration.s Worldwide. Crowned Miss Trans Global 2024, she draws strength from her rich mixed background spanning the West Indies, Asia, and Europe to champion equity and representation.

Change-making leadership vision:

To empower communities through inclusive, bold action that bridges cultures and transforms grassroots passion into sustainable global impact.



















René Fet (he/him)

 is a lifelong LGBTIQ+ activist, campaigner, professional gay, and community organiser with a refugee background, currently based in Luxembourg. Originally from Russia, he was at the forefront of the fight for LGBTIQ+ rights, co-organising Moscow Pride 20 years ago and challenging institutional homophobia through direct action, campaigning, and advocacy.

Change-making leadership vision:

To turn his lived experience, his voice, and his courage to speak up when others cannot safely do so into collective power — and use that power to change institutions, communities, and lives.



















Sean-Claude (he/him)

 is a Jamaican-born Creative Director, Curator, Storyteller and Community Organiser who migrated to the Netherlands as an asylum seeker in 2015. He is the founder of Freedom Work NL, a Black-trans-led DEIA (Diversity, Equity, Inclusion and Accountability) and creative consulting firm working towards LGBTQIA+ justice and Black liberation, and Man.ish Cave, an organisation supporting BPOC transmasculine people in and around Amsterdam.

Change-making leadership vision:

My change-making leadership vision is rooted in storytelling, liberation, healing, community building, and creating spaces where freedom becomes possible.



















Theodoros Vlachos (they/them)

 is from Greece and works independently as a social worker and researcher on trans and queer studies. They hold an interdisciplinary background in Social Work and International Relations (MSc, Aalborg University), with professional experience across humanitarian, community, NGO, and corporate settings, focused on child and adolescent protection, support for vulnerable groups, and Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DE&I) communications.

Change-making leadership vision:

To create spaces where lived experience becomes knowledge, participation becomes agency, and trans and gender-diverse people have the power to shape meaningful and lasting change.



















Tyler Dušak (they/them)

 is a queer transgender activist living in Croatia and a member of Zagreb Pride and Sjemenište kolektiv. Their focus is on building queer spaces where folk are welcome to express themselves and encouraging visibility and pride of all individuals in hopes of strengthening community efforts of transgender rights advocacy.

Change-making leadership vision:

Strength, compassion, and accountability with the ultimate goal of building a society with equality and equity for everyone and freedom from oppression at its forefront.



















Universe of Universal Friends (ey)

 is an intersectional trans activist in the Riga, LV area and beyond. With a focus on active inclusion and outreach, ey have been collaborating on the kviriem.lv queer resource and event compilation project, and running frequent, reliable trans community-building, artmaking, and connecting events.

Change-making leadership vision:

To make events  and connecting more accessible and enjoyable to a greater number of impoverished trans people, especially intersectionally oppressed trans women.



















Yuli Fernandez (she/her)

 is originally from Cuba and currently based in Greece. She is a Black trans woman, political refugee, migrant, and LGBTQIA+ activist living in Athens. She is a community facilitator, treasurer, and board member of her organisation, where she works to strengthen support, visibility, and inclusion for LGBTQIA+ people, particularly refugees, asylum seekers, and trans communities.

Change-making vision:

To turn lived experience into collective strength, create pathways for those who are often excluded, and build communities where everyone can lead with dignity and freedom.










Your support makes change possible




We work across Europe and Central Asia to advance trans rights, build strong communities, and drive change through research, advocacy, and community-building.




Your donation helps us continue this vital work — defending trans lives, amplifying trans voices, and advocating for justice every day.

author: TGEU
title: Hungary removes anti-LGBTI provisions, but trans people are still left out
content:
TGEU welcomes the decision of the Hungarian National Assembly on 13 October, 2026 to remove the anti-LGBTI content from the 2021 ‘child protection’ law. This is a necessary step to implement the Court of Justice of the EU (CJEU) judgment in 

Commission v Hungary

 (C-769/22).




In its April 2026 judgment, the CJEU found that the law, which stigmatised LGBTI people under the guise of child protection, breached EU law. It also rejected Hungary’s reliance on national identity to justify discriminatory measures. 




Why this matters for trans people




The ruling matters for trans people across the EU, because it confirms that Member States cannot use ‘child protection’ or national identity as an excuse for excluding trans and other LGBTI people from public life and the rights EU law guarantees them. The CJEU has already held in 

Mirin

 (C-4/23) that Member States must recognise a legal gender change obtained in another Member State, so the Commission has clear legal grounds to act. The CJEU has also held in 

Deldits

 (C-247/23) that a Hungarian refusal to rectify a trans refugee’s gender marker breaches the GDPR, which further strengthens the case for Commission action.




The reality of LGBTI rights in Hungary

author: Aoife Doran
title: Ceuta: Spain must protect trans asylum seekers, not return them to danger
content:
More than two months after tens of thousands of people crossed from Morocco into Ceuta, many remain in precarious conditions, with inadequate access to shelter, essential services and international protection. Among them are trans asylum applicants who have fled persecution, only to face further violence, insecurity and the threat of being returned to danger. Their situation is part of a wider humanitarian crisis affecting people on the move in Ceuta, all of whom deserve safety, dignity and access to protection.




We are deeply concerned by reports of physical assaults, harassment and mistreatment of people seeking protection in Ceuta. A 

report by Border Resistance

, a grassroots collective working at the border, documents at least seven alleged incidents of violence against LGBTI people between 21 August and 6 September. One trans woman described being assaulted by police officers after being expelled from a reception centre, stating, 

“We are trans, we cannot live on the street because we are attacked.”

 Another described fleeing Morocco after receiving death threats from her family. These testimonies expose the grave risks facing trans and other LGBTI people who seek protection in Ceuta, only to encounter further violence and insecurity. We also reject the racist and dehumanising portrayal of people arriving in Ceuta as an 

‘invasion’

author: TGEU
title: TGEU publishes Know Your Rights: How EU Directives Protect Trans People. Second Revised Version
content:
This guide provides a basic overview of EU directives in which trans people are protected from discrimination, including through the explicit inclusion of the grounds of ‘gender reassignment’, ‘gender identity’, or ‘gender expression’. As such, it helps trans people to better understand and claim their fundamental rights. It also helps legal professionals, equality bodies, and policymakers to understand their legal obligations to ensure equal protection. 










Get the guide










What are EU directives?




EU directives are a type of EU law that sets goals Member States must reach through their own legislation. However, EU directives do not prescribe how Member States should implement them. In other words, EU directives set a common minimum standard but leave Member States flexibility in how they achieve it.




All EU directives must be ‘transposed’, a process that incorporates an EU directive into national legislation. Once a directive is adopted, transposition begins, and the directive itself sets a deadline for completion.







Objective of the guide




Since TGEU published our first Know Your Rights guide in 2015, additional EU directives have been adopted and are entering into force. These newer directives, which extend protections for trans people across a broader range of areas, form the focus of this guide.







What does this guide cover?

author: TGEU
title: Join our webinar:  Countering Anti-Trans Misinformation – Tools, Tactics and Lessons from Across Europe
content:
Anti-trans misinformation is increasingly shaping public debates about trans rights across Europe. How do these narratives emerge, how do they travel across borders and platforms, and how can we respond effectively?




Join TGEU and the European Fact-Checking Standards Network (EFCSN) for a practical exchange between trans and LGBT organisations and fact-checkers from across Europe.




The webinar will explore common anti-trans misinformation narratives and how they are amplified and adapted in different contexts. It will also examine how fact-checking can help identify, contextualise, and respond to misleading claims.




Speakers from fact-checking organisations and TGEU members will share insights from their national and organisational contexts. A joint exercise and discussion will follow, focusing on approaches that can be adapted to different advocacy and communications contexts.




The session is an opportunity to learn from each other, build connections between the fact-checking and trans advocacy communities, and exchange practical approaches for responding to anti-trans misinformation online.




About the webinar




Date & time:

 12 November 2026, 10 – 11:30 CET

Location:

 Online via Zoom

Cost:

 Free

Target audience:

 TGEU members, trans and LGBT organisations, and activists

author: TGEU
title: Türkiye’s crackdown on LGBTI rights – the impact on trans people in prison
content:
Since 12 September 2026, Turkish authorities have intensified a nationwide crackdown on LGBTI people, organisations and human rights defenders. At least 117 people have reportedly been detained, with at least 83 held in pre-trial detention. 




The operation, branded “My Family is Safe” has involved arrests, raids on homes and organisations, digital restrictions, and the use of ‘public-morality’ and ‘obscenity’ provisions under Turkish criminal law. 







The impact on trans people




Criminalisation, discriminatory policing and restrictive prison practices in Türkiye come together to heighten risks for trans people in detention. At least 27 of those placed in pre-trial detention are trans women, many of whom have been charged with ‘prostitution’ and/or ‘obscenity’ offences. 




Trans detainees report strip searches and humiliating treatment and placement in detention arrangements that do not match their gender identity. Prison reports describe prolonged isolation, barriers to hormone treatment and HIV medication, limits on clothing and belongings, access to drinking water, overcrowding, and difficulty reaching legal and medical support.

author: Béla
title: Join our next PeerNetz session: building peer-led trans healthcare
content:
As part of our Peer Networking Zone (PeerNetz), TGEU is hosting a meeting to explore healthcare designed by and for trans people, rooted in community knowledge and care. We’ll be joined by Trans Healthcare Action, the organisation behind Kindred, Ireland’s first peer-led trans health clinic.




The session will be interactive, with practical exercises and space to explore how Kindred’s experience and lessons could translate to different contexts across Europe and Central Asia.




About the session




Date & time:

 

15 October, 16:00 – 17:30 CEST

Location:

 Online via Zoom

Cost:

 Free

Target audience:

 Trans communities and activists 










Register here










What the session will cover 




Trans Healthcare Actions will share how Kindred was created through co-creation between the local trans community and allied healthcare professionals, and walk us through the clinic’s foundation, model, structure, services and vision.




The session will also explore how the Irish social, legal and medical landscape shaped their approach, and invite participants to think about their own contexts: What gaps exist in trans healthcare? What community networks and resources are already available? What might help or hinder efforts to build similar community-led care?










Register here
